Bardolemeu Romeo - Backstory
Translated from PT-PT original provided by player (Tiago)

---

I was born into one of the richest and most influential families in the region. My family owned the largest theatres in the kingdom -- places where nobles, merchants, and important figures gathered to watch grand spectacles. From an early age, I was taught that art existed to generate profit, win favours, and strengthen our house's influence. Every play was carefully chosen to please the powerful, every musician hired was just another tool to maintain the family's prestige, and every round of applause was seen as a way to increase our wealth.

But I could never look at music that way.

While my parents treated artists like mere servants and discussed revenue, contracts, and political alliances, I found comfort in the company of an old musician who worked in one of our theatres. Unlike everyone else, he never treated me like an heir. He taught me to play the lute, to sing, and above all, he taught me that true art does not belong to the rich or the powerful. It belongs to the people. He often said that a good song could survive for centuries, long after any empire or fortune had crumbled.

As I grew older, I began to discover what truly sustained my family's prestige. Many artists were exploited -- paid little for their talent and discarded when they were no longer profitable. Shows were censored to please the nobles, stories were altered to protect influential figures, and anyone who dared to challenge the family's interests found their career destroyed. To my parents, art had no inherent value. It was merely a product.

The old musician knew too many secrets. He knew how artists were silenced, how plays disappeared on the orders of powerful people, and how fear was used to control those who depended on our theatres to survive. One day, he vanished without a trace. They told me he had decided to leave in search of new stages, but I never believed that lie. I am certain he was silenced for knowing more than he should.

In that moment, I realised that if I stayed in that house, I would end up becoming exactly like my parents.

That same night, I left the mansion without telling anyone. I took no jewellery, no gold, no part of the fortune that would one day be mine. I took only my master's old lute and the lessons he left me. I made a promise to myself: I would never allow art to serve only those who already had everything.

The early days were hard. I went hungry, slept in the open, and discovered a world completely different from the one I was raised in. But it was also in this world that I found what my master had always tried to teach me. I saw a simple song unite strangers in a tavern, draw a smile from children who had never set foot in a theatre, and restore hope to people who had lost everything. I understood that music did not exist to feed the egos of the powerful or enrich those who exploited it -- it existed to inspire, to comfort, and to remind people that they are never truly alone.

Since then, I have wandered without a fixed destination. Every song I compose is a tribute to the man who showed me the true meaning of art. Every story I tell seeks to immortalise the deeds of those who will never set foot on the stage of the great theatres or be remembered in the chronicles of the nobles. And every performance I offer freely to those who have nothing is a way of proving that art is worth more when it is shared than when it is sold.

Perhaps one day I will return to the theatres where I was born. Not to claim the inheritance I rejected, but to open the curtains to all those who were prevented from stepping onto the stage. I want to show my family that an artist's true legacy is not measured by the wealth they generate, nor by the applause of the nobility, but by the lives they are able to touch. After all, all the fortune in the world could never buy what they lost long ago: their humanity.
